title: Can an anonymous class extend a class and implement an interface simultaneously?
shortTitle: Can an anonymous class extend a class and implement an interface simultaneously?

s1_definition.profdef: No. An anonymous class has exactly one base type in its declaration — it can either extend a single class or implement a single interface, but never both at once, and never more than one interface. The `new Type() { ... }` syntax names exactly one supertype, so the compiler cannot express a combined "extends X and implements Y" anonymous declaration. If you need both, you must declare a named class, or implement an interface that itself extends the other type.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of an anonymous helper at National Bank of India who is given a single job description on a slip of paper. The slip can say either "act as a Teller" or "follow the Auditor rulebook," but it physically has room for only one role. If Rajesh's situation needs someone who is both a Teller and follows the Auditor rulebook at the same time, the branch cannot use a throwaway nameless helper — they must formally hire a named employee whose contract lists both roles. The nameless one-slip helper can wear only one hat.
s1_definition.oneliner: An anonymous class takes exactly one supertype — one class or one interface — so it can never extend a class and implement an interface at the same time.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** No. An anonymous class has exactly one base type in its declaration — it can either extend a single class or implement a single interface, but never both at once, and never more than one interface. The `new Type() { ... }` syntax names exactly one supertype, so the compiler cannot express a combined "extends X and implements Y" anonymous declaration. If you need both, you must declare a named class, or implement an interface that itself extends the other type.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of an anonymous helper at National Bank of India who is given a single job description on a slip of paper. The slip can say either "act as a Teller" or "follow the Auditor rulebook," but it physically has room for only one role. If Rajesh's situation needs someone who is both a Teller and follows the Auditor rulebook at the same time, the branch cannot use a throwaway nameless helper — they must formally hire a named employee whose contract lists both roles. The nameless one-slip helper can wear only one hat.

**One line to remember:** An anonymous class takes exactly one supertype — one class or one interface — so it can never extend a class and implement an interface at the same time.

sections.s2_technical:
The grammar of an anonymous class is `new SuperType(args) { body }`, where `SuperType` is a single class name or a single interface name. There is no syntactic slot for an `extends` clause combined with an `implements` clause. When `SuperType` is a class, the anonymous class extends that class and may use its constructor arguments. When `SuperType` is an interface, the anonymous class implements that one interface and the argument list must be empty, because interfaces have no constructor. In both cases only one supertype is written, so an anonymous class can never directly do both.

This is a real limitation compared to a named class, which can freely write `class AuditingTeller extends Teller implements Auditable, Serializable`. A named class may extend one class and implement many interfaces. An anonymous class is deliberately restricted to one supertype to keep the inline syntax simple and unambiguous.

There are two standard **work-arounds**. The first is to **create an interface that extends the interface you want**, or more usefully, define a single combined interface and have the anonymous class implement that. For example, if you want the behaviour of both `Auditable` and `Comparable`, define `interface AuditableComparable extends Auditable, Comparable<Trade> {}` and then `new AuditableComparable() { ... }`. Now the anonymous class implements a single interface that transitively requires both method sets. Interfaces can extend multiple interfaces, so this composes cleanly.

The second work-around is to **declare a named local class or a top-level class** that extends the class and implements the interfaces you need. The moment you need genuine multiple inheritance of type — one class plus one or more interfaces — the anonymous form is the wrong tool and a named class is correct.

A related point: an anonymous class that extends a class still only implements interfaces that the extended class already implements; you cannot add a brand new interface to it in the declaration. So if your base class `BaseProcessor` already implements `Runnable`, then `new BaseProcessor() { ... }` is a `BaseProcessor` and therefore also a `Runnable` by inheritance, but you did not add `Runnable` in the anonymous declaration — it came transitively from the base class. This is the only way an anonymous object ends up being both a subclass instance and an interface implementer, and it works precisely because the interface was already part of the single supertype you named.

A senior nuance is that this restriction is one reason people reach for named static nested classes or dedicated top-level classes in production code when a type must satisfy several contracts. In a bank's codebase, a settlement handler that must be both a domain `SettlementStrategy` and a Spring `ApplicationListener` cannot be an anonymous class satisfying both independently; it is written as a named class, which is also better for testing and readability.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India has a base class `BaseSettlementTask` that already implements `Runnable` so it can be scheduled, and the bank wants a one-off customised task. Because the base class already carries `Runnable`, an anonymous subclass of `BaseSettlementTask` is automatically both a `BaseSettlementTask` and a `Runnable`. This demonstrates the only legitimate way an anonymous class is "both" — by extending a class that already implements the interface.

Problem 2 — The bank then wants a throwaway object that is both `Auditable` and `Comparable` at the same time, which it cannot express as a single anonymous `new X() {}` across two independent types. We show the clean solution: define a combined interface `AuditableComparable` that extends both, and implement that single interface anonymously.

Problem 3 — Finally the bank needs a type that must extend a concrete `LedgerEntry` class and also implement a brand new `Exportable` interface at once. This is impossible anonymously, so we show the correct named-class solution, making the boundary of the rule concrete.

In the mini-project we build `BaseSettlementTask` implementing `Runnable`, interfaces `Auditable`, `Comparable`, a combined `AuditableComparable`, a `LedgerEntry` class and an `Exportable` interface, plus a named `ExportableLedgerEntry` class, and a `main` that demonstrates each case with logging.

The code contains: the base task, the interfaces, the combined interface, a named class for the impossible case, and demonstrations.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a trade TRD-1001 for 50,000 to be settled, plus ledger entry LED-1 for 50,000.

Step 1 — In CASE 1 we create an anonymous subclass of `BaseSettlementTask`, naming exactly one supertype. The compiler produces an object that is a `BaseSettlementTask`. Because `BaseSettlementTask` already implements `Runnable`, the object is also a `Runnable` by inheritance, which the `instanceof` check confirms as true.

Step 2 — We call `task.run()`. The inherited `Runnable.run` from the base class calls our overridden `settle`, which logs the settlement. This is the only legitimate sense in which an anonymous object is "both" — the interface was already carried by the single class we extended.

Step 3 — In CASE 2 we want a throwaway object that is both `Auditable` and `Comparable`. We cannot write two independent supertypes in one anonymous declaration, so we implement the combined interface `AuditableComparable`, which extends both. The anonymous class names one interface but must supply both `auditTrail` and `compareTo`.

Step 4 — In CASE 3 we need to extend the concrete `LedgerEntry` class and implement a brand new `Exportable` interface at the same time. This cannot be anonymous, so we use the named class `ExportableLedgerEntry`, and we export its line successfully.

```
2026-10-26 14:10:15 [INFO] CASE1 anon is BaseSettlementTask AND Runnable? true
2026-10-26 14:10:15 [INFO] Settling TRD-1001 amount Rs.50000
2026-10-26 14:10:15 [INFO] CASE2 anon implements combined interface: AUDIT: settlement TRD-1001
2026-10-26 14:10:15 [INFO] CASE3 named class export: LED-1,50000
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  CASE 1 — extend ONE class that already carries Runnable
    new BaseSettlementTask(...) { settle() }   ← ONE supertype named
       │ is-a BaseSettlementTask
       │ is-a Runnable (inherited, NOT a 2nd clause)
       ▼
    task.run() → settle() → log "Settling TRD-1001"

  CASE 2 — need Auditable + Comparable in a throwaway
    (Avoid) new Auditable() implements Comparable {}   ← NOT valid syntax
 interface AuditableComparable extends Auditable, Comparable
      new AuditableComparable() { auditTrail(); compareTo(); }  ← ONE interface

  CASE 3 — extend concrete class + implement NEW interface at once
    (Avoid) anonymous cannot do this
 class ExportableLedgerEntry extends LedgerEntry implements Exportable
      → exportLine() = "LED-1,50000"
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — One Supertype Rule ═══

  ┌─ Rule ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Anonymous: new X(){} → X is ONE class OR ONE interface        │
  │ Named class: extends 1 class + implements N interfaces OK     │
  │ Interface: can extend N interfaces (compose contracts)        │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │ <<interface>> Runnable   │        │ <<interface>> Auditable  │
  │ + run(): void            │        │ + auditTrail(): String   │
  └────────────┬─────────────┘        └────────────┬─────────────┘
               │ implemented by                    │ extended by
               ▼                                   ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │ BaseSettlementTask(abs)  │        │ <<interface>>            │
  │ - tradeId, amount        │        │ AuditableComparable      │
  │ + run() → settle()       │        │ extends Auditable,       │
  │ + settle() abstract      │        │         Comparable       │
  └────────────┬─────────────┘        └──────────────────────────┘
       extended anonymously
               ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │ anon{ settle() }         │  is-a BaseSettlementTask + Runnable
  └──────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ ExportableLedgerEntry (NAMED)                │
  │ extends LedgerEntry  ───▶ Exportable         │  ← the "both" case
  │ + exportLine(): String                        │     impossible anon
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Call Chain:
    1. new BaseSettlementTask(){settle} → instanceof Runnable = true
    2. task.run() → settle()
    3. new AuditableComparable(){auditTrail; compareTo}
    4. new ExportableLedgerEntry(...) → exportLine()
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
No, an anonymous class cannot extend a class and implement an interface at the same time, because the anonymous syntax names exactly one supertype. When I write new SomeType with a body, SomeType is either a single class or a single interface, and there is simply no place in that syntax to add a second extends or implements clause. A named class, by contrast, can extend one class and implement many interfaces, which is why the moment I truly need multiple type contracts I reach for a named class.

There is one subtle case that interviewers like to probe. An anonymous object can end up being both a subclass instance and an interface implementer, but only when the single class I extend already implements that interface. In my banking project I have a base settlement task that implements Runnable so it can be scheduled. When I create an anonymous subclass of that task, the object is a settlement task and also a Runnable, but Runnable came transitively from the base class, not from a second supertype I declared. I still named only one supertype.

When I genuinely need a throwaway object that satisfies two independent contracts, the clean solution is to define one combined interface that extends both, because interfaces are allowed to extend multiple interfaces. In my code I defined an auditable-and-comparable interface that extends both Auditable and Comparable, and then implemented that single combined interface anonymously, supplying both method sets. That respects the one-supertype rule while still giving me both behaviours.

And when I must extend a concrete class and implement a brand new interface at the same time, there is no anonymous way to express it, so I write a named class such as my exportable ledger entry that extends the ledger entry class and implements the exportable interface. In practice this is also better for a bank's codebase because named classes are easier to test, easier to read, and easier to reuse, so the one-supertype restriction on anonymous classes nudges me toward the right design rather than being a real obstacle.

---

keyPoints: Anonymous class: inline implementation with no name
Used for: one-time event handlers, callbacks, comparators
Can extend a class OR implement one interface (not both)
Captured variables must be effectively final
